gap: No result ChatGPT got sets a NAS price against what Dropbox costs: the Synology DS225+ body alone ($364.99 at Abt today, no drives) costs the same as 36.5 months of Dropbox Plus at $9.99/month (2 TB, 1 user, 30-day file recovery), and Synology Drive keeps up to 32 versions per file with rotation of up to 120 days, compared with Dropbox Plus's 30-day recovery.
standout_why: ChatGPT cited only Synology's Drive spec pages (synology.com/en-us and en-global, dsm/7.4/software_spec/synology_drive). I opened the en-us one. It gives the 32 versions and the 7/30/60/120-day rotation but no price and no Dropbox comparison. Neither do the other results, which are Synology KB pages, release notes and a 2020 white paper. ChatGPT's cards showed hardware prices from Best Buy, B&H and Walmart, but nothing tied them to the Dropbox bill the shopper wants to drop. The price-to-subscription comparison and the 30-day vs 120-day recovery gap appear on no result.
decides: It supports a 2-bay unit as the pick and puts a number on the payback. A NAS body costs about 20 to 37 months of Dropbox Plus before drives are added: UNAS 2 $199 ≈ 19.9 months, UGREEN DH2300 $239.99 ≈ 24.0, DS225+ $364.99 ≈ 36.5, DXP2800 $389.99 ≈ 39.0, F2-425 Plus $469.99 ≈ 47.0. A freelancer on the 2 TB Plus plan only comes out ahead after roughly three years or more, so the pick depends on the sync software more than on the hardware price. The DS225+ is not the cheapest box, but Synology documents on-demand files (Windows 10 1809+ and macOS 12.3+) and version retention up to 120 days, four times Dropbox Plus's 30. The Ubiquiti UNAS 2 and UGREEN DH2300 are cheaper; whether their sync software holds up is a question for another angle. UGREEN's own store prices the DXP2800 at $389.99, $25 more than the DS225+, so the 'good value' line in ChatGPT's answer depends on the $296.99 Walmart listing it showed, which I could not check.
